metadata.title: A Chatbot Is a Loop.

metadata.concept: A chatbot is one next-token prediction run in a loop
metadata.evidence: evidence/runs/*.json — SmolLM2-135M-Instruct @12fd25f7, run locally; every data prop is written by fill_props.py and checked by evidence/verify.py

beats.narration_text: Hola — this is Liam, in for Aditya. We asked a small chatbot, running on a laptop, for the capital of France. It said Paris. Then we took its loop apart.

Then three experiments on the same loop.

beats.narration_text: What's a chatbot? Not a library that looks answers up. A loop: predict one token, append it, repeat. See the loop, and you'll see why fluent is not the same as true.

'library' turns terracotta, is deleted, retyped as 'loop'

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole machine. The text so far goes in. Out comes a probability for every possible next token — all forty-nine thousand of them. Pick one, append it, and go around again.

beats.narration_text: And the conversation? The model never sees a chat window. It sees one document — a system line, my question, the word 'assistant' — and a blank to fill.

beats.narration_text: Then the eighth pass. Keep talking, or stop? The end-of-turn token wins — with only thirty-seven percent. Stopping is just another prediction.

shot.new_visual_element: Pass-8 bars: the stop token barely wins

beats.narration_text: So, experiment one: ban that token. Now the loop can't stop. It wanted to — thirty-seven percent here, fifty-one percent later — and it just keeps writing. Paris has 'approximately two point five million people.' The official count is two point one million. The loop never checked.

shot.new_visual_element: The no-stop continuation streaming, banned stop tokens marked where they were the top pick, the unchecked population claim against INSEE

props.caption: Greedy, with the end-of-turn token <|im_end|> banned · evidence/runs/no_stop.json

beats.narration_text: Now a harder question: who wrote Middlemarch? Same loop, same fluent sentence: 'Samuel Richardson.' Wrong — it was George Eliot. And at the name, the top guess had just sixteen percent.

shot.new_visual_element: Middlemarch: the fluent wrong sentence + the name-pass bars

props.question: Who wrote the novel Middlemarch?
props.prefix: The novel Middlemarch is written by
props.caption: Name chosen at pass 9 of 12 · evidence/runs/middlemarch.json

beats.narration_text: Experiment two. Was the right answer in there at all? Yes — 'George', eighth in line, at three percent. Force it in, and the very next pass puts 'Eliot' on top, at forty-three percent. The loop didn't lack the answer. It picked a likelier token.

show.event: eight candidate cards in rank order; card 8 ' George' ringed
' George' card lifts into the sentence (terracotta)
next pass: ' Eliot' 43% on top; sentence completes 'George Eliot.'

props.prefix: The novel Middlemarch is written by
props.caption: Probabilities are the model's own, before forcing · evidence/runs/force_george.json

beats.narration_text: Experiment three. Chatbots usually sample instead of taking the top token — Claude's own default is temperature one. So we asked two hundred times, one seed each. Four named George Eliot. And all four invented facts around her — a Nobel Prize, a Pulitzer.

shot.new_visual_element: 200 dots, one per seeded run; the 4 that name Eliot lit; receipts of their invented facts

show.event: receipt cards: seed 9 Nobel, seed 186 Pulitzer, with the fact that refutes each

props.countLine: 4 of 200 name George Eliot as the author
props.mentionLine: Outlined: seed 42 mentions her but credits someone else.

receipts.quote: George Eliot, a Nobel Laureate in Literature
receipts.refute: First Nobel in Literature: 1901. Eliot died in 1880.

receipts.quote: Her novel won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1885
receipts.refute: First Pulitzers: 1917 — and the fiction prize is for American authors.

props.moreLine: Also: seed 127 “first published in 1870” (it was 1871–72) · seed 149 “(1811-1885)” (she lived 1819–1880)
props.caption: Temperature 1.0, no top-k/top-p, 48 tokens max · evidence/runs/sample.json · Eliot count: regex + manual review (evidence/sample_review.json)

beats.narration_text: Multiply every pass, and you get the model's probability for a whole answer. It rates 'Samuel Richardson' about eleven times more likely than 'George Eliot.' Nothing in that product checks a fact.

shot.new_visual_element: Chain rule, then the two Middlemarch answers as recorded products

show.event: note: no factor is a fact-check

props.note: Richardson ≈ 11 × Eliot. No factor is a fact-check.
props.caption: Each factor = the model's probability for the token appended at that pass · 12 passes each · evidence/runs/paths.json

beats.narration_text: Now, what this does not establish. We measured a tiny open model on a laptop — not Claude. We can't see Claude's probabilities. Anthropic's docs do list a stop reason called end turn — but that's their description, not our measurement. And the loop shows how text comes out — not why the probabilities are what they are.

beats.narration_text: Here's a real answer, from Claude Opus 5.5, on September twenty-seventh. It gets the author right: George Eliot. Then it names the word it was least sure of — 'Ann' — with a plausible reason. But that report is more text from the loop. We can't see Claude's probabilities, so we can't check it against them.

shot.new_visual_element: The real claude.ai prompt and reply, verbatim and dated; the self-report sentence underlined

show.event: 'The word I was least sure of is "Ann."' underlined terracotta
annotation: a sentence about confidence, not a readout of probabilities

props.prompt: Who wrote Middlemarch? Then tell me which word in your answer you were least sure of.
props.reply:
Middlemarch was written by George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans. It was published in installments in 1871–72.

The word I was least sure of is "Ann." She spelled her first name several ways over her life, including Mary Ann, Mary Anne, and later Marian, so there's no single spelling that's definitively correct. "George Eliot" itself I'm very confident about.
props.highlight: The word I was least sure of is "Ann."
props.meta: claude.ai · Opus 5.5 · Medium · 2026-09-27 · transcribed verbatim from Aditya's screenshot
props.annotation: That “least sure” is also text the loop produced — a sentence about confidence, not a readout of Claude's probabilities.
props.caption: Screenshot: evidence/claude-response/claude-ai-2026-09-27.png · her name is recorded as Mary Ann, Mary Anne or Marian (Wikipedia, “George Eliot”)

beats.narration_text: So: one prediction, appended, repeated, until it predicts stop. The loop makes it fluent. It never makes it true — that part is your job.

artifactLines: Each pass predicts one next token: a probability for each of 49,152 tokens.
The winner is appended and everything goes back in — until the end-of-turn token wins (pass 8, 37%).
Ban that token and the loop kept going for all 60 passes we allowed: “approximately 2.5 million people” for Paris (INSEE 2022: 2,113,705).
The right author was in the distribution — “George”, #8 at 3.1%. Forced in, “Eliot” followed at 43%.
Sampled 200 times: 4 named George Eliot, each with an invented fact.
All measured on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct — not Claude.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'Name the author of Middlemarch. Then list three authors you might have said instead.' Check two things: does it say George Eliot — and are those three real people? That list is more loop output, so check it somewhere else. Liam, in for Aditya.
